title: Concision: cutting wordiness
note: Cut words that add nothing: redundant pairs (end result), redundant categories (red in color), filler (basically, kind of), slow openings (there are, it is important to note that) and nominalizations that bury the verb (make a decision for decide). Concise does not mean short; it means every word does work.

read.title: Make every word tell
text: William Strunk Jr. put the case for concision in 1918: "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts." He added that this does not require every sentence to be short, "but that he make every word tell."

Wordiness hides in predictable places. Redundant pairs say one thing twice: each and every, first and foremost, end result. Redundant categories name a class the reader already knows: red in color, a period of time. Slow openings make the reader wait: "It is important to note that" or "There are many people who."

The most damaging habit is burying actions in nouns. "The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy" contains two hidden verbs, decide and review. Released, the sentence becomes "The committee decided to review the policy," half as long and easier to follow. When you revise, hunt for nouns ending in -tion, -ment and -ance, and ask whether a verb is trapped inside.

q.q: According to Strunk, concision requires that...
What two hidden verbs does the reading find in the committee sentence?
